name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,367

clue.text: Deny scheme to capture European female

indicators.note: to capture something is to hold it inside, so the scheme word closes around the other letters

blocks.note: a ruse is a crafty scheme or trick

explanation.surface: Someone turns down a plot to kidnap a European woman.
explanation.definitionFit: To refuse a request is to decline or turn it down, the same verb sense as deny.

clue.text: Relocate right next to English market town

blocks.note: Settle is a market town in North Yorkshire

explanation.surface: Advice to move house to somewhere just beside an English market town.
explanation.walkthrough: Settle is a small market town in the Yorkshire Dales, at the start of the Settle-Carlisle railway.
explanation.definitionFit: To resettle people is to move them to a new home, a synonym for relocating them.

clue.text: Foul, ref! Thrill after 'e gives this

definitions.text: Foul, ref! Thrill after 'e gives this

indicators.note: something foul is spoiled or messed up, so the following short word is jumbled
after places the thrill word second, behind the dropped-h pronoun

blocks.note: 'e is 'he' with the h dropped, leaving just the letter E
a kick is a thrill, as in getting a kick out of something

explanation.surface: A fan yells at the referee to award a free kick after a foul, with 'e standing for the official.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition as well: after a foul, the referee awards exactly this. 'After' means the thrill comes behind the E.
explanation.definitionFit: In football a free kick is the restart awarded to a side whose player was fouled.

clue.text: Wild tiger seen? Not here

indicators.note: wild letters are out of control and scattered, ready to be put in a new order

explanation.surface: A safari-goer asks whether they might spot a tiger in the wild and is told not in this place.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: tigers live in Asia, so you will never see a wild one on the African plains of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Serengeti is the great Tanzanian savanna, famous for lions and wildebeest but with no tigers at all.

clue.text: Freak accident of cat with dog barking

indicators.note: barking is British slang for mad, and mad letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A strange mishap involving a cat and a yapping dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barking' looks like what the dog is doing, but it means mad. The letters of 'of cat' and 'dog' are mixed together.
explanation.definitionFit: An act of God is an unforeseeable natural event, a legal phrase for a freak accident nobody caused.

clue.text: Sophisticated male with work in foreign locations

indicators.note: something foreign is strange and unfamiliar, so the following word is made strange by rearrangement
the short words placed in the longer one go inside it

blocks.note: op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A worldly man whose job takes him to places abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: Cosmopolitan describes a worldly, urbane person familiar with many cultures, which is what sophisticated means.

clue.text: Hope Radamès embraces Aida?

definitions.note: Aida is an example, hence the question mark

indicators.note: the two words embrace the answer by holding it within them across their join

blocks.note: the letters sit across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the hero Radamès will take Aida in his arms.
explanation.walkthrough: Radamès is the hero of Verdi's Aida, so the whole clue paints a scene from the work itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Aida is Verdi's opera of 1871, so it is an example of the genre, signalled by the question mark.

clue.text: Extremely large drink after good chat

indicators.note: after sends the size and drink pieces behind the abbreviation for good

blocks.note: OS stands for outsize, a clothing size for very large
to sip is to drink a little

explanation.surface: A big drink taken after a good natter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After good' puts the G first; OS is the clothing label for outsize.
explanation.definitionFit: Gossip is idle talk about other people, a kind of chat or natter.

clue.text: Challenging sweetheart to drop Latin

indicators.note: dropping something leaves it out, so a letter goes

blocks.note: darling is an endearment for a sweetheart

explanation.surface: A demanding loved one who wants to give up Latin lessons.
explanation.definitionFit: A daring act is bold and provocative, so challenging in the sense of defying convention.

clue.text: Sticks earth in boxes

indicators.note: the earth letter is placed in the boxing word

blocks.note: to spar is to box in practice

explanation.surface: Someone pushes sticks into soil stored in crates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxes' looks like containers but is a verb for fighting; 'Sticks' is a verb too.
explanation.definitionFit: To spear something is to pierce or stab it, as one sticks a fork into food.

clue.text: Bottoms almost tender, one judges

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: asses is US slang for bottoms

explanation.surface: Sore backsides belong to someone who sits in judgement all day.
explanation.definitionFit: An assessor is a person who evaluates or appraises things, someone appointed to judge them.

clue.text: Finished almost first in state - one's exceptionally successful

indicators.note: almost means not quite complete, so the leader word loses its last letter
the shortened word sits in the word for declaring

blocks.note: to aver is to state firmly

explanation.surface: Coming close to top place in the state exams marks out a star pupil.
explanation.definitionFit: An overachiever does better than expected, a person whose success goes beyond the normal level.

clue.text: Captured a king in trap when retreating

indicators.note: the short pieces are put in the trap word
retreating means going backwards, so the trap word is read from right to left

blocks.note: a net is a trap for fish or birds
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A monarch caught in an ambush while his army fell back.
explanation.definitionFit: Taken is the past participle of take in its sense of seize or capture a prisoner.

clue.text: Breaking instrument? It's flipping working!

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the short word is read backwards

blocks.note: the viola is a stringed instrument
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: Someone smashes a musical instrument while exclaiming that the wretched thing does work after all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British curse but tells you to turn the little word round.
explanation.definitionFit: A violation is a breach of a rule or law, the noun form of breaking it.

clue.text: Pants - or more - found in rugby players' changing areas?

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, so the words it governs are a mess and get rearranged
something found in another sits inside it

blocks.note: locks are second-row forwards in a rugby scrum

explanation.surface: Underpants, and more, left lying about where the rugby team gets changed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' looks like clothing, apt for a changing room, but it is British slang for rubbish and signals the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Locker rooms are where teams change clothes before and after games, so they are areas for changing.

clue.text: Sends husband article on exercises to get trim

blocks.note: to ship goods is to send them
PE is physical education, school exercises

explanation.surface: A wife packs her husband off to work out so he gets in shape.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the earlier pieces above the exercises.
explanation.definitionFit: Shipshape means neat and in good order, which is one sense of the adjective trim.

clue.text: Woodwork happened to be holding in bed

indicators.note: holding something keeps it inside, so the verb word goes around the little word

blocks.note: a cot is a small bed

explanation.surface: Someone who happened to be in bed was tucked up there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In bed' reads as one phrase, but 'in' is held and 'bed' follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Wainscot is wooden panelling on the lower part of a room's walls, a piece of woodwork.

clue.text: Paid Steel lousily? Independent's ignored column's support

indicators.note: doing something lousily means doing it badly, so the letters are jumbled
what is ignored is left out, so that letter is dropped

explanation.surface: A newspaper columnist complains of being paid badly by Steel, the Independent having ignored them.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedestal is the base on which a column or statue stands, so it supports the column.

clue.text: Grass on blanket after Pluto leaves

indicators.note: when someone leaves they go away, so those letters disappear

blocks.note: blanket coverage is indiscriminate, applying to all
Dis is another name for Pluto, Roman god of the underworld

explanation.surface: An informer tells on someone once the dog Pluto has gone, or perhaps the planet.
explanation.walkthrough: Dis is the Roman underworld god also called Pluto; 'grass' is British slang for an informer.
explanation.definitionFit: To grass on someone is British slang for informing against them, which is to incriminate them.

clue.text: Son about to be trapped by rascal, getting frightened

indicators.note: being trapped by something means being held inside it

blocks.note: a cad is a rascal or bounder

explanation.surface: A boy about to be cornered by a scoundrel grows fearful.
explanation.definitionFit: Scared and frightened are direct synonyms describing someone filled with fear.

clue.text: Area next to slum housing unknown refugee's goal?

indicators.note: housing something gives it a home inside, so the letter goes within

explanation.surface: A district beside a slum that shelters an unidentified displaced person.
explanation.definitionFit: Refugees seek asylum, the protection and refuge granted by a foreign state, so it is what they aim for.

clue.text: Country clubs with old celebrity in charge opening in Aberdeen

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its start, so only the first letter is taken

blocks.note: C is the card abbreviation for clubs
IC is the abbreviation for in charge
the first letter of the Scottish city

explanation.surface: A veteran celebrity who runs golf clubs is opening a new venue in Aberdeen.
explanation.definitionFit: Costa Rica is a Central American country between Nicaragua and Panama.

clue.text: Player about to lob over hill

indicators.note: to lob something is to toss it up and over, so the word is turned upside down

blocks.note: ca is short for circa, about
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A tennis player is about to send a lob high over a hill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to' reads as 'on the point of', but 'about' is the piece and 'to lob' turns it over; in a down clue 'over' places it above the hill.
explanation.definitionFit: A player is a performer on stage, so it is an informal synonym for an actor.

clue.text: Individual ignoring large burn

indicators.note: ignoring something leaves it out, so that letter is removed

explanation.surface: One person pays no attention to a big burn.
explanation.definitionFit: To singe is to burn something slightly on its surface or edges.

clue.text: Recall clutching at dad?

definitions.note: dad is an example, hence the question mark

indicators.note: clutching means gripping, so the first word holds the second inside

blocks.note: to relive is to recall a past experience vividly

explanation.surface: Remembering grabbing hold of one's father.
explanation.definitionFit: A dad is one example of a relative, a member of the family by blood or marriage.

clue.text: Tycoon's large Jaguar?

blocks.note: a jaguar is a big cat, an example hence the question mark

explanation.surface: A mogul's big Jaguar car.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the luxury car a tycoon might drive, but the jaguar is the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A fat cat is a slang term for a wealthy, powerful business person, which is a tycoon.

clue.text: Editor spins in front of me with sort of skirt? That's sweet!

definitions.note: the answer is a sugar, a sweet thing

indicators.note: spinning turns something round, so the abbreviation is read backwards

blocks.note: a rara is a short layered frilly skirt

explanation.surface: An editor twirls in front of the speaker wearing a frilly skirt, and the speaker finds it charming.
explanation.definitionFit: Demerara is a light brown cane sugar, so it is something sweet used in coffee and baking.

clue.text: Refusal to have time for one concerned with teeth

indicators.note: to have one thing for another is to swap it in, so a letter is replaced

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone who works on teeth says they have no time for anyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One concerned with teeth' looks like a dentist, but 'one' is the letter swapped out.
explanation.definitionFit: Dental is the adjective for anything relating to teeth or dentistry.
